## Overview

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapters 1–6; Franklin (2009), chapter 10. Practical execution order, rather than a repetition of lecture theory. -->

Fit SDMs to two simulated case studies:

- Central Asian otter (1-D river network)
- Desert monitor lizard (2-D survey area)

Using the same 8-step workflow:

1. Define the question and prediction region.
2. Check occurrences and environmental rasters.
3. Sample background and extract predictor values.
4. Reserve a spatial test and check predictors.
5. Fit the model and inspect its response curves.
6. Evaluate withheld records.
7. Map suitability and flag extrapolation.
8. Export results with their interpretation.

# Case study 1: Otters

## 1. Define the otter prediction target

<!-- Sources: Original simulation in code/simulate_sdm_data.R; Franklin (2009), chapters 4–5. The practical's independent raster exercise is not the small transect subset used to illustrate concepts in 01_sdms.qmd. Instructor preparation is saved separately in notes/instructor/prepare_otter_sdm.R and is not part of the student walkthrough. -->

**Question:** which river-corridor cells have potentially suitable otter habitat?

- We use a 500 m grid, riparian cover (%) and elevation (km) to fit a SDM.
- Compare verified autumn presence locations with background.

```{r otter-region, out.height="1.25in"}
preview_river <- rast("data/river_mask.tif")
map_plot(preview_river,"Prediction region: simulated river corridor")
```

## 2. Load the prepared otter presence data

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), sections 2.2–2.4. Independent SDM simulation; instructor-only preparation removes invalid and duplicate-cell records and transforms coordinates before class. -->

```{r read-records, echo=TRUE}
records <- read.csv("data/otter_sdm_presences.csv")
head(records[, c("record_id", "x", "y")], 3)
```

- There are **`r nrow(records)` verified simulated sign locations**, from autumn
2025.
- One record per 500 m cell (duplicates removed). 
- Coordinates are in metres:
`x` is easting; `y` is northing, in UTM zone 43N (EPSG:32643).


## 2. Load and check the raster layers

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 4.1; terra rast/compareGeom documentation. All environmental values synthetic. -->

```{r rasters, echo=TRUE}
# load raster layers
env <- rast("data/environment.tif")
river <- rast("data/river_mask.tif")
names(env)
```

```{r rasters2, echo=TRUE}
res(env) # check resolution
stopifnot(compareGeom(env, river)) # check if same CRS
```

```{r rasters3, echo=TRUE}
# `vect()` turns `x` and `y` into map points.
pres <- vect(records, geom=c("x", "y"), crs=crs(env)) 
```

- `cover`: percent riparian cover; `elev_km`: elevation in kilometres;
`temperature`: in degrees C.
- `river` is a mask with 1's in river-corridor cells and missing elsewhere.

## 2. Inspect the cleaned presence map

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapter 2; Franklin (2009), chapter 4. Original schematic. -->

```{r clean-map, out.width="60%"}
map_plot(river,"Verified presence cells (simulated)",pres)
```

Look for:

- isolated errors, 
- dense clusters,
- large unsampled areas.

## 3. Sample background within the corridor

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapter 3; Merow et al. (2013), section III.A and III.D; terra spatSample documentation. -->

```{r background, echo=TRUE}
set.seed(410)
bg <- spatSample(river, size=600, method="random",
  na.rm=TRUE, as.points=TRUE, values=FALSE)
nrow(bg)
```

- Background samples available river environments, including some recorded cells.
- Uniform sampling is suitable recording effort was uniform; non-uniform recording may need non-uniform background selection.
- `set.seed()` makes random sampling repeatable. 
- Background locations are not unsuccessful surveys.

## 3. Extract predictors and build the table

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 4.2; terra extract documentation. -->

```{r extract, echo=TRUE}
p <- extract(env, pres, ID=FALSE)
b <- extract(env, bg, ID=FALSE)
p$pb <- 1; b$pb <- 0
p$x <- crds(pres)[,1]; b$x <- crds(bg)[,1]
p$y <- crds(pres)[,2]; b$y <- crds(bg)[,2]
dat <- rbind(p,b)
stopifnot(all(complete.cases(dat)))
```

`ID=FALSE` prevents an extraction row number becoming a predictor.
`pb=0` means background. Missing habitat values must be investigated.

## 3. Check the table before fitting

<!-- Original student checkpoint. Presence/background labels match the theory lecture; no survey absence is inferred. -->

```{r table-check, echo=TRUE}
head(dat[, c("pb", "cover", "elev_km")], 3)
```

```{r table-check2, echo=TRUE}
table(dat$pb)
```

**Discuss:** if a background location has excellent habitat, should its label
change to 1?

## 4. Reserve a spatial test dataset before fitting

<!-- Sources: Franklin (2009), chapters 6 and 9; Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapter 7; Roberts et al. (2017). Single predeclared split; not a validated otter spacing rule. -->

```{r holdout, echo=TRUE}
train <- subset(dat, x < 329000)
test <- subset(dat, x >= 330000)
# 329000 <= x < 330000 is a 1 km buffer.
rbind(training=table(train$pb),test=table(test$pb))
```

- `subset()` keeps rows meeting a condition. 
- Both presences and background are split. No cell enters both sets.
- Points with $329000\leq x < 330000$ are not included in train or test.
- This buffer is to avoid any spatial dependence between train and test sets.
- Buffer size is illustrative here; must be chosen with study system in mind.

## 4. Inspect the training and test regions

<!-- Sources: Franklin (2009), chapter 9; Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapter 7. Original split diagram. -->

```{r holdout-map}
map_plot(river,"Western training region; eastern test region")
rect(329000,4370000,330000,4400000,col=adjustcolor('grey40',.4),border=NA)
points(train$x,train$y,pch=16,col=bl,cex=.4)
points(test$x,test$y,pch=16,col=rd,cex=.4)
abline(v=c(329000,330000),lty=2)
```

## 4. Check predictors in the training data

<!-- Sources: Dormann (2011), collinearity; Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 4.2; Franklin (2009), chapter 5. -->

```{r cor, echo=TRUE}
round(cor(train[,c("cover","elev_km","temperature")]),2)
```

Elevation and temperature contain almost the same information here.
We retain **elevation**, as planned, and leave temperature out.

- Use ecological reasoning and data quality as well as correlation.
- Do not change predictor choices repeatedly after looking at test performance.

## 5. Fit a simple starting model

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 6.3.1; Franklin (2009), section 6.3; R stats::glm documentation. -->

```{r linear, echo=TRUE}
m_linear <- glm(pb ~ cover + elev_km,
  family=binomial(), data=train)
stopifnot(m_linear$converged)
```

- `glm()` fits a generalised linear model.
- `binomial()` selects logistic regression for the 0/1 response.
- `data=train` protects the withheld records.

The fitted value distinguishes presence rows from background rows.


## 5. Compare a quadratic model

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), sections 5.1 and 6.3; Dormann (2011), model formulation/simplification. Predeclared main model avoids test-based tuning. -->

```{r quadratic, echo=TRUE}
m_curve <- glm(pb ~ cover + elev_km + I(elev_km^2),
  family=binomial(), data=train)
AIC(m_linear, m_curve)
```

- `I(elev_km^2)` adds a squared term so the elevation effect can be curved.
- These models use exactly the same rows and background sample.
- Lower AIC indicates relative support, not proof of good fit to data.
- Here simpler linear model is preferred.

## 5. Read a response curve

<!-- Sources: Dormann (2011), section 13.2.3 and Figure 13.3; Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 5.2. Approximate conditional Wald interval. -->

```{r cover-curve-code, echo=TRUE}
# generate covariate values to predict pb for
curve_data <- data.frame(
  cover=seq(min(train$cover),max(train$cover),length.out=100),
  elev_km=median(train$elev_km))
# predictions of pb
pr <- predict(m_curve, curve_data, type="link", se.fit=TRUE)
# summaries to plot
curve_data$score <- plogis(pr$fit)   # mean prediction
curve_data$low <- plogis(pr$fit-1.96*pr$se.fit)  # LCL
curve_data$high <- plogis(pr$fit+1.96*pr$se.fit) # UCL
```

- Calculates predictions across the observed cover range.
- Hold other covariates (elevation) constant at its training median.
- Curve shows how response changes as cover changes.

## 5. Inspect both fitted response curves

<!-- Sources: Dormann (2011), section 13.2.3; Franklin (2009), chapter 9. Original fitted simulation. -->

```{r cover-curve}
style(c(1,2)); z<-curve_data
par(mar=c(4.5,4.6,2,.8), mgp=c(3.1,.7,0))
plot(z$cover,z$score,type='n',ylim=range(z$low,z$high),
 xlab='Riparian cover (%)',ylab='Presence-background score')
polygon(c(z$cover,rev(z$cover)),c(z$low,rev(z$high)),
 col=adjustcolor(bl,.2),border=NA)
lines(z$cover,z$score,col=bl,lwd=3)
rug(train$cover[train$pb==1],col=rd)
e <- data.frame(cover=median(train$cover),
 elev_km=seq(min(train$elev_km),max(train$elev_km),length.out=100))
e$score <- predict(m_curve,e,type="response")
plot(e$elev_km,e$score,type="l",lwd=3,col=bl,
 xlab="Elevation (km)",ylab="Presence-background score")
rug(train$elev_km[train$pb==1],col=rd)
```

- Each curve holds the other predictor at its training median. 
- Red ticks show elevations where presences were recorded.
- The shaded band is a 95% confidence interval.

## 6. Evaluate model on the test dataset

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 5.3 (rank-based AUC); Franklin (2009), chapter 9. Helper in code/helpers.R. -->

```{r test-predict, echo=TRUE}
test$score <- predict(m_curve,test,type="response")
p_test <- test$score[test$pb==1]
b_test <- test$score[test$pb==0]
auc_test <- auc_pb(p_test,b_test)
round(auc_test,3)
```

AUC compares `r length(p_test)` withheld presence cells with
`r length(b_test)` background locations in the eastern block.
Here, 0.5 means chance ranking; 1 means every test presence ranks above
every test background location. It is not the percentage of sites correct.

## 6. Check what the AUC result supports

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 5.3; Franklin (2009), chapter 9. Original fitted results. -->

```{r scores}
style(); boxplot(list(Background=b_test,Presence=p_test),
 col=c('grey80',bl),ylab='Presence-background score',
 main=paste('Withheld eastern block: AUC =',round(auc_test,2)))
```

Overlap means some presences receive low scores and some background locations
receive high scores. Remember background may contain otters.

Held-out AUC is **`r round(auc_test,2)`**, with `r length(p_test)` test presences.
This is weak discrimination: investigate records, predictors and sampling before
using the map for habitat decisions.

## 7. Predict suitability across the river network

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), sections 5.2 and 6.3; terra predict/mask documentation. -->

```{r map-predict, echo=TRUE}
predictors <- mask(env[[c("cover","elev_km")]],river)
score_map <- predict(predictors,m_curve,
  type="response",na.rm=TRUE)
names(score_map) <- "presence_background_score"
```

- `terra::predict()` applies the fitted relationship cell by cell.
- Predictor names match the model formula.
- Covariate values outside the river mask don't get predictions.


## 7. Flag extrapolation before interpreting the map

<!-- Sources: SEEC 1 extrapolation/MESS; Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 6.5; Franklin (2009), chapters 9–10. Deliberately limited univariate range screen. -->

```{r novelty-code, echo=TRUE}
outside <- predictors[[1]] < min(train$cover) |
           predictors[[1]] > max(train$cover) |
           predictors[[2]] < min(train$elev_km) |
           predictors[[2]] > max(train$elev_km)
flagged <- global(outside,"sum",na.rm=TRUE)[1,1]
flagged
```

- This simple screen flags at least one predictor outside its training range.
- It cannot detect every novel **combination** of values within those ranges.
- More complete environmental-overlap checks are advisable for real projects.

## 7. Inspect the score and extrapolation maps

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), sections 5.2 and 6.5; Franklin (2009), chapter 10; original simulation. -->

```{r score-map, out.width="100%", out.height="1.45in"}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
map_plot(score_map,"Otter habitat score (simulated)",pres)
map_plot(outside,"Outside training ranges",zlim=c(0,1))
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

- Left: darker cells have higher scores; dots are presence records.
- Right: TRUE flags areas where extrapolation is happening (`r flagged` river cells).

These maps show relative habitat suitability, not abundance or occupancy.

# Case study 2: Desert monitors

## 1. Define a polygon-based prediction region

<!-- Sources: Original simulation in code/simulate_monitor_sdm_data.R; Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapters 3–4. All region geometry and species records are fictional. -->

**Question:** where is potentially suitable desert-monitor habitat within
this hypothetical survey region?

Use the same eight steps. Replace the river corridor with a polygon,
and the habitat rasters with two climate layers on a 1 km grid.

```{r monitor-region, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.1, out.width="72%", out.height="1.25in"}
mon_region <- vect("data/monitor_sdm/survey_region.gpkg")
mon_mask <- rast("data/monitor_sdm/region_mask.tif")
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
plot(mon_region,col='grey92',border=bl,axes=FALSE,
 main='Hypothetical survey region',mar=c(.3,.3,1.5,.3))
```

## 2. Load the monitor records and BIOCLIM rasters

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), sections 2.5 and 4.1–4.2; WorldClim definitions https://www.worldclim.org/data/bioclim.html. Synthetic files generated by code/simulate_monitor_sdm_data.R, not downloaded WorldClim climate values. -->

```{r monitor-load, echo=TRUE}
# load rasters
mon_raw <- read.csv("data/monitor_sdm/records.csv")
mon_env <- rast("data/monitor_sdm/bioclim.tif")
# transforms longitude/latitude into the raster's coordinates
mon_pres <- project(vect(mon_raw,
 geom=c("longitude","latitude"), crs="EPSG:4326"), crs(mon_env))
# remove duplicate presences
mon_cells <- cellFromXY(mon_env, crds(mon_pres))
mon_pres <- mon_pres[!duplicated(mon_cells), ]
# perform checks
stopifnot(compareGeom(mon_env,mon_mask))
stopifnot(all(!is.na(extract(mon_mask,mon_pres)[,2])))
```

- **`r nrow(mon_pres)`** presences after removing duplicates.
- `bio6`: minimum temperature of coldest month (degrees C).
- `bio12`: annual precipitation (mm). Every value is synthetic.
- **Discuss**: what do the checks do?

## 2. Inspect the climate maps and presence overlay

<!-- Sources: Original climate gradients in code/simulate_monitor_sdm_data.R; Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapter 4. -->

```{r monitor-climate, fig.height=3.1, out.width="100%", out.height="1.45in"}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
map_plot(mon_env[["bio6"]],"BIO6 (degrees C)",mon_pres)
lines(mon_region,lwd=1)
map_plot(mon_env[["bio12"]],"BIO12 (mm)",mon_pres)
lines(mon_region,lwd=1)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

Check alignment, units, missing cells and predictor coverage.

## 3. Sample polygon background and extract values

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapters 3–4; terra spatSample/extract. Uniform background matches the simulation's constant recording effort. -->

Here we create the presence and background data by:

- sampling the background points and adding covariates,
- extracting presence locations and adding covariates,
- combining the two

```{r monitor-background, echo=TRUE}
set.seed(420)
# construct background dataset
mon_bg <- spatSample(mon_mask, 1200, method="random",
 na.rm=TRUE, as.points=TRUE, values=FALSE)
mb <- extract(mon_env, mon_bg, ID=FALSE)
mb$pb <- 0  # add response
mb$x <- crds(mon_bg)[,1]; mb$y <- crds(mon_bg)[,2]
# construct presence dataset
mp <- extract(mon_env, mon_pres,ID=FALSE)
mp$pb <- 1  # add response
mp$x <- crds(mon_pres)[,1]; mp$y <- crds(mon_pres)[,2]
# combine
mon_dat <- rbind(mp,mb)
```

## 4. Reserve a spatial test dataset 

<!-- Sources: Franklin (2009), chapter 9; Hijmans & Elith (2023), chapter 7. Fixed demonstration split chosen before model fitting, not tuned to its AUC. -->

```{r monitor-split, echo=TRUE}
mon_train <- subset(mon_dat,x < 550000)
mon_test <- subset(mon_dat,x >= 552000)
# 550000 <= x < 552000: a 2 km buffer.
rbind(training=table(mon_train$pb),test=table(mon_test$pb))
round(cor(mon_train[,c("bio6","bio12")]),2)
```

- Check that training data represent the test region's climates.
- Real projects need several spatial folds.

## 5. Fit SDMs

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 6.3; Franklin (2009), chapter 6. Intermediate optima are deliberately built into the simulation; no empirical claim about monitors. -->

```{r monitor-fit, echo=TRUE}
mon_model <- glm(pb ~ bio6 + I(bio6^2) +
                      bio12 + I(bio12^2),
                 family = binomial(),
                 data = mon_train)
```

- We simulated data so presences are concentrated in warm, relatively dry climates.
- This is only for illustration; real relationships may be very different.

## 5. Inspect the fitted climate responses

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 5.2; Dormann (2011), interpretation. Conditional fitted curves from synthetic data. -->

```{r monitor-curves}
style(c(1,2))
par(mar=c(4.5,4.6,2,.8), mgp=c(3.1,.7,0))
for(v in c("bio6","bio12")) {
 curve_mon <- data.frame(bio6=median(mon_train$bio6),
                        bio12=median(mon_train$bio12))
 curve_mon <- curve_mon[rep(1,100), ]
 curve_mon[[v]] <- seq(min(mon_train[[v]]),max(mon_train[[v]]),length.out=100)
 plot(curve_mon[[v]],predict(mon_model,curve_mon,type="response"),
      type='l',lwd=3,col=bl,ylab='Presence-background score',
      xlab=if(v=="bio6") 'BIO6 (degrees C)' else 'BIO12 (mm)')
 rug(mon_train[[v]][mon_train$pb==1],col=rd)
}
```

- Each curve holds the other predictor at its training median.
- Red ticks indicate covariate values at presence locations.

## 6. Evaluate model on the test dataset

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 5.3; Franklin (2009), chapter 9. Same presence-background AUC definition as in the otter example. -->

Monitor AUC compares `r sum(mon_test$pb == 1)` withheld presences with
`r sum(mon_test$pb == 0)` background cells.

```{r monitor-evaluate, echo=TRUE}
mon_test$score <- predict(mon_model,mon_test,type="response")
mon_p_test <- mon_test$score[mon_test$pb==1]
mon_b_test <- mon_test$score[mon_test$pb==0]
mon_auc <- auc_pb(mon_p_test,mon_b_test)
round(c(mon_auc),3)
```

```{r monitor-scores}
style(); boxplot(list(Background=mon_b_test,Presence=mon_p_test),
 col=c('grey80',bl),ylab='Presence-background score',
 main=paste('Test set AUC =',round(mon_auc,2)))
```

Strong separation between scores of presences and background locations.

## 7. Predict across the polygon and flag extrapolation

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), sections 5.2 and 6.5; terra predict/mask. Range screening matches the otter procedure, not a full multivariate novelty test. -->

Predict habitat suitability across the survey region:

```{r monitor-map-code, echo=TRUE}
mon_score <- mask(predict(mon_env,mon_model,
 type="response",na.rm=TRUE), mon_mask)
names(mon_score) <- "presence_background_score"
```

Flag test areas with covariate values outside the training data:

```{r monitor-map-code2, echo=TRUE}
mon_outside <- mon_env[["bio6"]] < min(mon_train$bio6) |
 mon_env[["bio6"]] > max(mon_train$bio6) |
 mon_env[["bio12"]] < min(mon_train$bio12) |
 mon_env[["bio12"]] > max(mon_train$bio12)
mon_outside <- mask(mon_outside, mon_mask)
```

## 7. Inspect the score and extrapolation maps

<!-- Sources: Original evaluated monitor model; Franklin (2009), chapter 10. Map fitted on training records only. -->

```{r monitor-map, fig.height=3.4, out.width="100%", out.height="1.45in"}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
map_plot(mon_score,"Monitor habitat score (simulated)",mon_pres)
lines(mon_region,lwd=1)
map_plot(mon_outside,"Training-range extrapolation",zlim=c(0,1))
lines(mon_region,lwd=1)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

- **Left**: Darker cells have higher relative scores. Dots are supplied records.
- **Right**: True flags a value outside a training range.

# Export the results

## 8. Export the score and extrapolation maps

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), reproducible R workflow; Franklin (2009), chapter 10. Current outputs use output/practical/. -->

```{r export-maps, echo=TRUE}
writeRaster(score_map,
 file.path(out_dir,"otter_score.tif"),overwrite=TRUE)
writeRaster(outside,
 file.path(out_dir,"otter_extrapolation.tif"),overwrite=TRUE)
writeRaster(mon_score,
 file.path(out_dir,"monitor_score.tif"),overwrite=TRUE)
writeRaster(mon_outside,
 file.path(out_dir,"monitor_extrapolation.tif"),overwrite=TRUE)
```

The four GeoTIFF files can be opened in a GIS. Keep each score map with
its extrapolation flag. `overwrite=TRUE` replaces earlier exercise outputs.

## 8. Save the models and evaluation records

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), reproducible R workflow; Franklin (2009), chapter 10. -->

```{r export-tables, echo=TRUE}
saveRDS(list(otter=m_curve,monitor=mon_model),
        file.path(out_dir,"glm_models.rds"))
write.csv(test,
 file.path(out_dir,"otter_test.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(mon_test,
 file.path(out_dir,"monitor_test.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()),
 file.path(out_dir,"sessionInfo.txt"))
```

Keep the question, region, units, background, model formula, spatial test,
AUC and limitations with the exported files.

# Optional: compare GLM with MaxEnt

## Optional: fit MaxEnt to the same training data

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 6.4.1; Merow et al. (2013), features/regularisation; official maxnet documentation. R implementation needs no Java. -->

```{r maxnet-fit, echo=TRUE, eval=requireNamespace("maxnet", quietly=TRUE)}
library(maxnet)
xvars <- c("cover","elev_km")
mx <- maxnet(train$pb,train[,xvars],
  f=maxnet.formula(train$pb,train[,xvars],classes="lq"),
  regmult=1)
```

- `lq` allows linear and quadratic features.
- `regmult` controls regularisation.
- This uses the same training data, predictors and background as the GLM.
- These settings are a starting point, not validated settings.

## Optional: evaluate MaxEnt using the same test

<!-- Sources: Hijmans & Elith (2023), section 5.3; Merow et al. (2013), model complexity/output scale; maxnet predict documentation. -->

```{r maxnet-test, echo=TRUE, eval=requireNamespace("maxnet", quietly=TRUE)}
mx_test <- as.numeric(predict(mx,test[,xvars],
                              type="link",clamp=FALSE))
mx_auc <- auc_pb(mx_test[test$pb==1],mx_test[test$pb==0])
round(c(GLM=auc_test,MaxEnt=mx_auc),3)
```

- AUC needs rankings, so predictions can be on link or response scale.
- Numerical GLM and MaxEnt scores as not comparable.
- Do not choose MaxEnt settings based on the test data (use another dataset for this).
- Do not choose preferred models based on the test data (use another dataset for this).
- No difference in predictive accuracy of the two approaches here.
